data.title: Just Four Days Till Gildan Activewear Inc. (TSE:GIL) Will Be Trading Ex-Dividend
data.description:
It looks like Gildan Activewear Inc. (TSE:GIL) is about to go ex-dividend in the next 4 days. Typically, the ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important because any transaction on a stock needs to have been settled before the record date in order to be eligible for a dividend. Therefore, if you purchase Gildan Activewear's shares on or after the 25th of November, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 21st of December.

The company's upcoming dividend is US$0.249 a share, following on from the last 12 months, when the company distributed a total of US$1.00 per share to shareholders. Last year's total dividend payments show that Gildan Activewear has a trailing yield of 2.9% on the current share price of CA$48.73. We love seeing companies pay a dividend, but it's also important to be sure that laying the golden eggs isn't going to kill our golden goose! So we need to check whether the dividend payments are covered, and if earnings are growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Gildan Activewear is paying out an acceptable 51% of its profit, a common payout level among most companies. A useful secondary check can be to evaluate whether Gildan Activewear generated enough free cash flow to afford its dividend. Luckily it paid out just 19% of its free cash flow last year.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

See our latest analysis for Gildan Activewear

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with shrinking earnings are tricky from a dividend perspective. Investors love dividends, so if earnings fall and the dividend is reduced, expect a stock to be sold off heavily at the same time. Gildan Activewear's earnings per share have fallen at approximately 9.0% a year over the previous five years. Such a sharp decline casts doubt on the future sustainability of the dividend.

The main way most investors will assess a company's dividend prospects is by checking the historical rate of dividend growth. Since the start of our data, 10 years ago, Gildan Activewear has lifted its dividend by approximately 12% a year on average. Growing the dividend payout ratio while earnings are declining can deliver nice returns for a while, but it's always worth checking for when the company can't increase the payout ratio any more - because then the music stops.

The Bottom Line

Has Gildan Activewear got what it takes to maintain its dividend payments? We're not enthused by the declining earnings per share, although at least the company's payout ratio is within a reasonable range, meaning it may not be at imminent risk of a dividend cut. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy Gildan Activewear today.

If you're not too concerned about Gildan Activewear's ability to pay dividends, you should still be mindful of some of the other risks that this business faces. Every company has risks, and we've spotted 5 warning signs for Gildan Activewear you should know about.

If you're in the market for strong dividend payers, we recommend checking our selection of top dividend stocks.

data.title: Analyst Estimates: Here's What Brokers Think Of The Walt Disney Company (NYSE:DIS) After Its Yearly Report
data.description:
The full-year results for The Walt Disney Company (NYSE:DIS) were released last week, making it a good time to revisit its performance. Results were roughly in line with estimates, with revenues of US$102b and statutory earnings per share of US$5.63. This is an important time for investors, as they can track a company's performance in its report, look at what experts are forecasting for next year, and see if there has been any change to expectations for the business. Readers will be glad to know we've aggregated the latest statutory forecasts to see whether the analysts have changed their mind on Walt Disney after the latest results.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Taking into account the latest results, the most recent consensus for Walt Disney from 27 analysts is for revenues of US$106.7b in 2027. If met, it would imply an okay 4.2% increase on its revenue over the past 12 months. Per-share earnings are expected to expand 19% to US$6.91. Yet prior to the latest earnings, the analysts had been anticipated revenues of US$106.1b and earnings per share (EPS) of US$6.69 in 2027. The analysts seems to have become more bullish on the business, judging by their new earnings per share estimates.

Check out our latest analysis for Walt Disney

There's been no major changes to the consensus price target of US$131, suggesting that the improved earnings per share outlook is not enough to have a long-term positive impact on the stock's valuation. There's another way to think about price targets though, and that's to look at the range of price targets put forward by analysts, because a wide range of estimates could suggest a diverse view on possible outcomes for the business. The most optimistic Walt Disney analyst has a price target of US$144 per share, while the most pessimistic values it at US$86.00. There are definitely some different views on the stock, but the range of estimates is not wide enough as to imply that the situation is unforecastable, in our view.

One way to get more context on these forecasts is to look at how they compare to both past performance, and how other companies in the same industry are performing. It's pretty clear that there is an expectation that Walt Disney's revenue growth will slow down substantially, with revenues to the end of 2027 expected to display 4.2% growth on an annualised basis. This is compared to a historical growth rate of 6.0% over the past five years. Compare this against other companies (with analyst forecasts) in the industry, which are in aggregate expected to see revenue growth of 8.2% annually. Factoring in the forecast slowdown in growth, it seems obvious that Walt Disney is also expected to grow slower than other industry participants.

The Bottom Line

The most important thing here is that the analysts upgraded their earnings per share estimates, suggesting that there has been a clear increase in optimism towards Walt Disney following these results. On the plus side, there were no major changes to revenue estimates; although forecasts imply they will perform worse than the wider industry. The consensus price target held steady at US$131, with the latest estimates not enough to have an impact on their price targets.

With that said, the long-term trajectory of the company's earnings is a lot more important than next year. We have forecasts for Walt Disney going out to 2029, and you can see them free on our platform here.

Still, Quanta Services faces two obvious pressure points: a potential pause in hyperscaler capex and any squeeze in copper and equipment supply that crimps project delivery.

data.title: How This Defense Stock Is Creating Solutions To Modern Warfare
data.description:
By 2027, the US military aims to spend more than US$1 billion on a program to procure hundreds of thousands of drones, highlighting how quickly unmanned systems are becoming part of modern warfare.

Drones are transforming the battlefield.

A small first-person view (FPV) drone, which can cost less than US$10,000, can potentially destroy military assets such as tanks and radar systems worth many times its purchase price. This creates an unusual equation for defense spending where relatively inexpensive weapons can threaten some of the most expensive equipment on the battlefield.

This has led to drone stocks becoming a major focus for investors interested in defense exposure.

This has captured the attention of US defense stock First Breach (FBDT), which is looking to mass-produce two models of drones for military purposes.

Drones are a growing area for defense stocks

According to Grand View Research, the US drone market is expected to grow from US$25.1 billion in 2024 to US$52.5 billion by 2030, equivalent to annual growth of around 13%.

The global market is forecast to expand from approximately US$73 billion to US$163 billion over the same period, representing annual growth of 14.3%. These estimates cover the wider drone industry, including commercial applications, but illustrate the scale of the opportunity as adoption expands.

Military procurement is adding to this demand. The US Drone Dominance programme has allocated US$1.1 billion for prototype orders, with the US Army outlining plans involving approximately 340,000 drones.

First Breach hopes to capture some of this opportunity with two proprietary platforms: the Close-Quarters Strike (CQS) and Long Range Strike (LRS).

The CQS is designed for close-range operations, with a demonstrated range of around 2 kilometres and a 500-gram payload. The LRS targets a range exceeding 20 kilometres and a payload of approximately one kilogram, completing its first test flight in October 2026.

First Breach aims to begin scaled production in Q2 2027, eventually reaching a capacity of more than 2,500 drones per week. However, it has yet to report drone revenue or disclose production orders.

Old-fashioned ammunition still necessary

Although drones might be a critical defense technology, traditional technology like ammunition remains important.

According to First Breach, the US market for ammunition is expected to grow just under 12% per year to US$12.1 billion by 2031. Looking specifically at defense spending, in the recent US Army budget, an extra US$7.3 billion was requested to expand munitions, including ammunition.

First Breach is hoping to take advantage of this growth, increasing its market share and expanding its product lines. The company plans to transition to 24-hour production, increasing production capacity by 175%. This will allow the company to manufacture up to 20 million rounds per month.

Helping this increase is a recent agreement with SAS Ammo, an ammunition retailer and wholesaler, that is popular amongst recreational and competitive shooters as well as law enforcement. Under the agreement, the minimum monthly purchase will increase from 3 million rounds to 8 million rounds for a period of three years.

This growth might start to flow through.

In its recent third-quarter result, revenue from ammunition sales rose to $568,856 from $45,853 a year earlier and was 57% above the $361,357 recorded in the first half of 2026 and nearly six times the $95,353 recorded in the second quarter.

First Breach betting on two sides of modern warfare

First Breach is looking to build a footprint in two fast-growing, critical sections of the defense market.

It starts with its established ammunition business where the company aims to increase output, improve manufacturing scale and expand its customer base both in America and overseas. While it does this, it also aims to grow its drone business from the ground up with scaled production targeted for the second quarter of 2027, and eventual capacity of 2,500 drones per week.

The most-followed narrative on the Simply Wall St community is built around the potential of this combination. It argues that First Breach's ammunition operations, growing sales and developing drone platforms could position it to benefit from increased defense spending and demand for expendable military equipment.

data.title: Why Buffalo Potash's First Mine Could Be Just The Beginning
data.description:
Saskatchewan-based potash stock, Buffalo Potash (TSXV:BUFF), could be building something much bigger than its first mine suggests.

The company’s Disley project is being developed in stages, beginning with what the company calls its initial production module or IPM, which is designed to produce around 125,000 tonnes of potash annually.

However, that is just the beginning.

Two proposed follow-on facilities could eventually take the project's planned annual production capacity to 1.125 million tonnes, making the initial module a relatively small part of Buffalo's longer-term ambitions.

The big question is whether Buffalo can use this initial development to establish the foundations for a much larger potash business.

Buffalo Potash’s first steps

Buffalo Potash has decided that rather than jumping into developing a mine capable of full production, it would instead start small.

The initial production module is a smaller-scale mining facility designed to produce around 125,000 tonnes of soluble-grade potash annually. This means that rather than committing to the full Disley project, it is choosing to start with a facility capable of providing initial cash flow, with lower capital requirements as it establishes the foundation for future expansion.

This module will use Buffalo’s patented horizontal line drive technology.

In simple terms, this approach involves drilling three horizontal wells along an underground potash seam. This approach promises lower upfront capital requirements, lower operating costs, more selective extraction, and less infrastructure requirements.

Progress has moved beyond the planning stage. Buffalo Potash has received approval to construct and operate the initial production module in October 2026, subsequently commencing brine injection, the first test of whether Buffalo can make its method work, as well as beginning site development.

First production remains targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

For Buffalo, getting this first facility operational could be an important step towards demonstrating the technology and supporting the case for a much larger Disley development.

How two more mines could transform Buffalo’s Disley Project

Buffalo Potash's real growth opportunity lies not in its initial production module, but in what the company plans to come after.

It plans to build two additional facilities, Disley East and Disley West, each designed to produce around 500,000 tonnes of potash annually. If both proceed, this would add 1 million tonnes of annual capacity, taking the Disley Project’s planned total production from 125,000 to 1.125 million tonnes. This would be a welcome addition to a market which is considered by many countries to be a critical mineral.

There is also a difference in what the facilities would produce.

While the IPM is designed to produce soluble-grade potash, the two larger operations are intended to produce granular muriate of potash (MOP), a more widely used fertiliser product. This would give Buffalo a pathway into a much larger-scale production operation, with the potential to contribute to the growing opportunity for Canadian potash producers.

The results of the IPM will go a long way in determining how successful and viable Buffalo’s expansion could be.

At full capacity, the two proposed mines would produce eight times as much potash as the initial module, illustrating just how much larger Buffalo's ambitions could become.

More than just a first mine

Buffalo’s long-term ambitions are vast, but much of it relies on the success of its initial production module.

Given that the Disley Project is located in Saskatchewan, which is already a major global hub of potash production, its proximity to major mines and infrastructure is a positive. But until it starts showing that it can produce potash profitably, such ambitions will remain largely potential rather than reality.

But that potential is there, and interest is already building, with the company announcing that seven state-owned enterprises and major private companies have reached out to Buffalo Potash seeking new sources of Potash supply.

The most-followed narrative in the Simply Wall St community for Buffalo Potash highlights the company's opportunity to bring new Canadian potash supply to market using a potentially lower-cost mining method. It also points to the recent regulatory approval and proposed C$8.5 million royalty funding agreement with Altius Minerals as important steps towards getting the first module operational.

There is no question that Buffalo’s ambition is large and that the opportunity is there given the increasing importance placed on potash as a key ingredient of fertilizer. Investors will, however, be focused on execution.
